_notes: District EdTech usage listing — 1:1 device programs, platforms, AI tools/policies, notable services, contracts, and student-data-privacy agreements. Compiled from district technology pages, handbooks, school-committee minutes, budget documents, local press, and the SDPC/Massachusetts Student Privacy Alliance registry (sdpc.a4l.org). A signed privacy agreement means a tool was vetted for use, not proof of active classroom deployment. Listing only — no rating or tiering.

publicCommentary.who: Patrick Larkin, Burlington High School principal
publicCommentary.what: Told the school committee the 1:1 iPad rollout — the first in the state to give every high schooler an iPad — was putting Burlington in the national spotlight: 'There is no roadmap when distributing 1,000 iPads to students for the first time. We are creating the roadmap.' Announced a student-run tech help desk (Educational Technology Integration course).

publicCommentary.who: Eric Conti, superintendent

aiPolicy.summary: No districtwide AI policy as of spring 2026. Until then, individual Cambridge schools regulate AI use independently; the May 2026 screen-usage coverage reiterated that no district-wide AI policy exists yet.

publicCommentary.who: Caitlin Dube, School Committee Vice Chair
publicCommentary.what: Co-sponsored an April 2026 resolution to suspend non-essential student-facing screen use for pre-K through grade 2; said 'Screens are not neutral, especially for early childhood learners' and 'You only get to be 5 once.' The motion was deferred to Superintendent Murphy pending the district's screen-usage audit.

publicCommentary.who: Luisa de Paula Santos, School Committee member (resolution co-sponsor)
publicCommentary.what: Questioned what screen use is 'absolutely necessary' versus relying on screens 'as a crutch'; later noted the district's usage study lacks evidence that screen time improves learning and does not capture smartboards.

publicCommentary.who: David Murphy, Superintendent
publicCommentary.what: Warned against using technology 'by default'; after the pause resolution was deferred to him, suggested enforcing existing guidance restricting screens as behavioral rewards.

publicCommentary.who: Chris Montero, Cambridge Education Association president
publicCommentary.what: Pushed back on the proposed early-grades screen ban, calling a sudden ban 'not helpful to anybody'; union technology specialist/VP Sarah Rosenberg emphasized that 'quality' of screen use matters.

publicCommentary.who: Heather Francis, Executive Director of Academics (district screen-usage audit)
publicCommentary.what: Presented the 23-day April-May 2026 audit: median Chromebook use rises from 17 min (kindergarten) to 71 min (high school); K-5 use is 98-99% instructional but falls to ~85% at the high school. Full report due June 2026. Committee member Elizabeth Hudson requested immediate action steps rather than waiting.

publicCommentary.who: Richard Harding, School Committee member
publicCommentary.what: On the AI resolution: 'AI is gonna be here, it's a powerful tool... we are actually behind in our policy on AI.' Parent Gabriel Robinson opposed the resolution's premise, arguing students should prioritize 'core skills and knowledge independent of those tools.'

publicCommentary.who: Boston Globe (Christopher Huffaker) — statewide context
publicCommentary.what: Cambridge named among Massachusetts communities in the 'anti-Chromebook movement' — the Globe reported school officials in Cambridge were weighing a ban on screens for the youngest grades amid parent concern.

aiPolicy.summary: Formal AI guidance under School Committee policies IJNDB (Technology Acceptable Use) and IJNDC (Acceptable Use of Digital Resources, adopted January 2025). Rules include: never share personal information with AI models; 'Always double-check information from AI. You are responsible for the accuracy of your work'; unpermitted AI use is plagiarism and permitted use requires citation. An AI Steering Committee (formed Nov 2023; 23 members in 2025-26 including 10 parents and 5 students) maintains the S.H.I.E.L.D. student framework, a red/yellow/green assignment-labeling system for AI permissions, a privacy-first mandate against entering PII into AI tools, and deepfake reporting protocols.

aiPolicy.summary: First-ever generative-AI policy adopted April 8, 2025 (policy subcommittee 3-0, full School Committee 5-0). Policy states the district "will incorporate the teaching and use of genAI into relevant aspects of the K-12 curriculum" and directs administration to create "sound, grade-appropriate (procedures or) guidelines to help support the wise and ethical use of genAI by teachers and students," covering responsible use, prohibited use, academic integrity, and safety/security/privacy. Adoption led directly to a partnership with MIT's Day of AI team and former DESE Commissioner Jeffrey C. Riley.

aiPolicy.summary: No adopted district AI policy found. On 2026-01-29 the School Committee's Standing Committee on Teaching, Learning and Student Success took up items to require explicit parent/guardian consent before third-party services use student data to train AI or collect biometric data (audio, photos, video); the administration opposed new policy, saying every approved app 'must meet strict data privacy and safety standards' via 'legally binding Student Data Privacy Agreements.'

publicCommentary.who: Noelia M. Chafoya, Aislinn Doyle, and Catherine Holmes — founding members, Worcester for Safe Student Technology (parent advocacy group)
publicCommentary.what: Telegram & Gazette guest column criticizing 'overreliance on school-issued iPads and Chromebooks' and 'passive screen viewing during instructional and noninstructional time'; called for removing daily internet-connected device use in preK-2, intentional tech instruction, transparency on tech contracts and evidence of academic benefit, and informed parental consent before data collection — citing LAUSD and Cambridge School Committee as precedents.

publicCommentary.who: Worcester School Committee (Standing Committee on Teaching, Learning and Student Success)
publicCommentary.what: Considered items requiring explicit parental consent before student data is used to train AI and before biometric data collection; superintendent's administration argued existing Student Data Privacy Agreement vetting already suffices.
